title: Clinical Mastery: Altitudinal Visual Field Defects
summary: An altitudinal visual field defect is a semi-circular loss of the superior or inferior visual field, typically indicating pathology along the visual pathway from the optic nerve to the chiasm. Rapid identification is critical to prevent permanent vision loss in ischemic and compressive conditions.

sections.title: Definition & Topography
sections.content: An altitudinal defect is a visual field loss that respects the horizontal meridian. Superior altitudinal defects are classically associated with inferior optic nerve/retinal pathology, while inferior altitudinal defects result from superior involvement. Unlike hemianopias, these defects are primarily pre-chiasmal in origin.

rows: Axonal loss at the lamina cribrosa

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Panic
content: ESR > 50mm/hr or CRP elevated (Giant Cell Arteritis)
Altitudinal defect in a patient > 50 with jaw claudication

content.explanation: P: Pill (Viagra/PDE5i), A: Age > 50, I: Ischemic/Inflammatory, N: Nocturnal hypotension, S: Small cup-to-disc ratio (disc-at-risk)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workflow
content: Step 1: Confrontation Fields & Automated Perimetry (24-2 or 30-2 HFA).
Step 2: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the optic nerve head (assess for cupping vs. edema).
Step 3: Blood panel (ESR, CRP, CBC, Glucose) if GCA or Diabetes suspected.
Step 4: Neuro-imaging (MRI Brain/Orbit with Gadolinium) if compression is suspected.
Step 5: OCT Optic Nerve Head (check RNFL thickness) and OCT-Angiography.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: In NAION, the visual field defect is classically inferior, but can be central or arcuate.
A 'disc-at-risk' is defined as a small vertical cup-to-disc ratio < 0.2.
Always check blood pressure; nocturnal systemic hypotension is a major risk factor for ischemic optic neuropathy.
In glaucoma, altitudinal defects usually occur in advanced stages (Stage 4+).
